title: How Is This Even Possible?
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey summarizes a recorded panel he hosted with several higher-education AI thinkers, built around a recent book on transparency and reflection in student and AI work. The panelists agree that terms like "AI literacy" and "responsible AI" are too vague to be useful without institutional definitions. They disagree on what should count as evidence of learning once a polished product no longer shows what a student knows: the arc across a semester, captured process, or an acceptance that cognition was never directly visible. Reflection is treated as valuable but suspect as evidence when students know it is graded. Tim and Mike push the group away from a single right approach toward asking what fits these learners, this task and this stage, and the discussion closes on faculty capacity and institutional change. The post is a recap that raises more questions than answers, set in higher education rather than K-12.
points: The panel treats "AI literacy" and "responsible AI" as vague labels, so institutions must define what students and faculty should actually know or do.
Because AI makes a polished product a weak signal of learning, the group splits among reading the arc of a semester, capturing process, and admitting cognition was never directly visible.
Reflection helps less-experienced students examine their choices, but it becomes unreliable evidence when students know the instructor is grading it.
The better question is not which AI pedagogy is right but what suits these learners, this task and this point in their development.
Faculty need time, support and a stronger grasp of how people learn before widespread pedagogical change is realistic.
quotes: AI makes it much harder to infer what a student knows from a polished final product. The disagreement was over what, if anything, should replace that evidence.
Look across a semester rather than at a single artifact. Students document their AI use, work through increasingly difficult tasks, and reflect on the accumulated evidence.
Cognition was never directly visible. We inferred it from student work. Asking students to explain their thinking does not necessarily give us access to what actually happened.
Reflection becomes problematic as evidence when students know an instructor is reading and grading it. Students have incentives to produce the reflection the instructor wants.
The practical question becomes less “What is the right AI pedagogy?” and more “What makes sense for these learners, doing this task, at this point in their development?

Higher education has a tendency to overcomplicate things. Students still need knowledge and practice. Apprenticeship, feedback, mastery, and other established approaches already provide useful models.
Faculty need time, space, and support to learn and redesign their teaching. AI cannot simply become another responsibility added to an already full workload.
We had considerably more agreement that these are the questions than we did about the answers.
